sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Ohio homestead exemption
sections.html:
The exemption goes to owner-occupants who are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, or the surviving spouse of someone in those groups. A disabled veteran, a disabled veteran's surviving spouse, and the surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty get their own larger reduction. The definitions sit in R.C. 323.151.

Age is counted in a particular way. For this purpose, "sixty-five years of age or older" means a person who reached 64 before January 1 of the year of application. In practice a senior owner must be 65 by December 31 of the year the application is filed.

The home itself has to meet several tests:

  • It is a dwelling the applicant owns and occupies as a home, with Ohio as the domicile.
  • It includes the surrounding land only up to one acre that is reasonably needed for the home.
  • It was not acquired from a relative, other than a spouse, for the purpose of qualifying.
  • An owner can be a life tenant, a vendee in possession under a land contract, a mortgagor, or the settlor of a trust that holds title to a home the settlor occupies.

Homes held by corporations, partnerships and LLCs generally do not qualify, because the owner is not an individual.

sections.h2: How much the exemption takes off the bill
sections.html:
It works as a credit on the property tax bill, figured on a slice of the home's market value. The size of the credit also depends on the local tax rate: the higher the rate, the higher the credit. The reduction amounts are indexed for inflation each year.

Homestead reduction amounts and income limit, tax year 2026 (real property)
Owner groupTax year 2026 amount
Low-income senior or disabled owner$29,700
Disabled veteran, or surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty$59,400
Income threshold for seniors and disabled owners$41,000

Income is measured by modified adjusted gross income, which the statute defines for the owner and spouse for the year before the application.

No income test applies to a disabled veteran, a disabled veteran's surviving spouse, or the surviving spouse of a public service officer. Owners who received the exemption in 2013, before means testing returned, are also outside the income test.

File with the auditor of the county where the home sits, on or before December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Three forms are in use: DTE 105A for most applicants, DTE 105I for a disabled veteran or that veteran's surviving spouse, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers. Every county auditor must take a paper copy, and some accept electronic filing.

A disability claim needs a certificate. R.C. 323.153 calls for a physician's certificate for a physical disability, and a physician or psychologist who practices in Ohio for a mental one. A certificate from a state or federal agency that classifies disability also works. A veteran attaches written confirmation of the disability rating from the federal VA.

After filing, the sequence runs like this:

  • The auditor approves or denies the application and sends notice within thirty days of that decision.
  • A denial notice must state the reasons.
  • An owner who thinks the denial was wrong, or the reduction too small, can appeal to the county board of revision within sixty days of the notice, using form DTE 106B.
  • Each January the auditor mails a continuing application. Send it back only if ownership, occupancy, disability or income changed.

A false statement made to get the reduction is a fourth-degree misdemeanor and bars the reduction for three years after a conviction.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell
sections.html:
The reduction follows the owner, not the house. Under R.C. 323.152(C), a transfer of ownership after an application was filed does not forfeit the reduction for that year. Once the home is sold, though, the seller no longer owns or occupies it, so the continuing application should go back to the auditor reporting the change.

Failing to report costs money. If the auditor or treasurer finds that an owner kept a reduction after losing eligibility, a charge goes on the property for each affected tax year, with interest as if the reduction were delinquent tax. It is collected like delinquent taxes, which makes it something a title company will catch at closing.

The buyer starts from a different place. The partial exemption in R.C. 323.152(B)(2) calls for a fresh application when a home changed hands in the preceding year, and the auditor mails an original application each February for homes that transferred. The filing deadline is again December 31. A senior or disabled buyer who moves in must apply at the new address, beginning in January of the year after the move. Ownership and occupancy as of January 1 decide the tax year.

Three other pieces of relief show up on Ohio residential bills. The first is the partial exemption under R.C. 319.302, which the auditor reviews parcel by parcel as of January 1. For residential property it is listed at seven and one-half percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, with later steps ending at zero percent for and after the third following tax year. Ask the auditor what percentage applies to a given bill.

The second is the owner-occupancy credit, a reduction on a primary residence occupied on January 1 of the application year. Ask the auditor whether it already appears on your bill.

The third is a county option created by House Bill 96, signed in June 2025. County commissioners may adopt a local-option homestead exemption that mirrors the state one, with the same eligibility rules and the same amount. Nobody applies for it separately: anyone already getting the state exemption receives it automatically once a county turns it on. The auditor can tell you whether your county has done so.

Farmland has its own track, the Current Agricultural Use Value program, which also runs through the auditor.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has the exemption
sections.html:
The exemption rarely changes the sale itself, but it shows up in the tax figures on the settlement statement. A seller who has been receiving the credit should bring the most recent tax bill to closing, since the credit appears there. A buyer who plans to live in the house should ask the title company how the owner-occupancy filing is handled at the county auditor's conveyance step.

A few practical points for sellers:

  • An heir who inherits a home does not get the seller's reduction automatically. Eligibility depends on the new owner's own age, disability and occupancy.
  • A home under a land contract can still qualify, because R.C. 323.151 counts a vendee in possession as an owner.
  • Pending appeals and unpaid installments are matters for the county treasurer, who bills and collects the tax.

Back taxes, a tenant or heavy repairs are separate problems from the exemption. A cash sale skips showings and repair negotiations, and the title company still handles any tax proration at closing.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply for the Ohio homestead exemption every year?
faqs.a: No. Once approved, the application continues for each year the dwelling is your homestead. The auditor mails a continuing application each January, and you return it only if your income, ownership, occupancy or disability status changed.

faqs.q: What is the last day to file the Ohio homestead exemption for real property?
faqs.a: December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Manufactured and mobile homes taxed that way file by December 31 of the year before. The statute allows a late application for the preceding year to be filed with an original application.

faqs.q: Can I get the Ohio homestead exemption if my home is in a trust?
faqs.a: Often yes. Revocable and irrevocable trusts can qualify when the trust gives you complete possession of the property. Check the trust language with the county auditor before applying.

faqs.q: Who decides the Ohio homestead exemption, and where do I appeal?
faqs.a: The county auditor decides it. If you believe the denial or the amount is wrong, file a complaint with the county board of revision within sixty days of the auditor's notice.

faqs.q: Does selling my Ohio home end the exemption?
faqs.a: Yes, for future years. The reduction applies to a home you own and occupy, so tell the auditor when you no longer qualify. Skipping that step can lead to a charge on the property with interest for years the reduction should not have been given.
